tweets: GPT-3, Gwern writes, is an old 2018-style architecture scaled up 117-fold from GPT-2 — and that scale-up alone produced meta-learning: the ability to follow instructions and learn new tasks from a few examples, not just more memorized facts.

Before GPT-3, Gwern expected scaling curves to bend around 100 billion parameters. Instead GPT-3's 175 billion parameters kept following the same smooth power-law improvement, suggesting trillion-parameter models remain within reach.

GPT-3 is expensive by machine-learning standards — training cost estimated around $5m, plus heavy storage and running costs — but Gwern argues that's still cheap next to major scientific or military budgets, so further scaling is plausible.

Gwern calls this the 'blessings of scale': across image, game, robotics and language models, bigger models and data tend to become more stable, generalize better, and spontaneously meta-learn — the opposite of the rule that bigger problems are harder.

Gwern's explanation: a large network contains many smaller sub-models layered inside it. Those that memorize or use shortcuts learn fastest, but enough data and scale eventually favor sub-models that encode genuine, general algorithms.

This supports what Gwern calls the strong scaling hypothesis: once a flexible, brain-like architecture exists, simply training ever-larger versions on more data lets sophisticated behavior emerge naturally, with no special new algorithm required.

The 'pretraining thesis': minimizing error at predicting the next character forces a model from letter frequencies, to spelling, word associations, and finally sentences that make sense, each gain requiring deeper understanding.

Gwern argues the hardest-won reductions in prediction error are the most valuable, requiring reasoning, causality and theory of mind — though he admits the argument, while logically clean, offers no guarantee it keeps working as models scale further.

Gwern estimates a GPT-3-successor trained with another 100-1000x compute would still fall short of human-level prediction accuracy by his calculation — and notes that no one, including him, can say what capabilities such a jump would actually produce.

Whether an AI arms race starts now, Gwern argues, depends less on who has the hardware — Google and DeepMind already do — than on who has the organizational conviction that scaling alone will work; right now, almost nobody beyond OpenAI is betting on it.

DeepMind, Gwern writes, holds a 'weak' version of the hypothesis: it expects to need to reverse-engineer the brain module by module. OpenAI instead bet its whole organization on the stronger claim that scale alone suffices.

Looking back, Gwern notes that respected AI researchers confidently predicted stagnation through 2014-2016, warning of an 'AI winter' — and were wrong, with few ever revisiting or retracting those predictions.

Gwern pushes back on dismissing models as 'just' statistics: if intelligence is ever built from simple mechanisms, success must look exactly like reducing a hard capability to 'just' a well-defined algorithm — that's the goal, not a refutation.

In an appendix, Gwern argues agency is not on/off but a continuum: training a model on human-generated text full of agents planning and acting can make it capable of planning and acting when prompted — filtering out 'agentic' data may not remove this.

Even abstract systems like Conway's Game of Life or random Turing machines, Gwern suggests, can push a model toward agent-like reasoning — chunking cells into 'gliders', or inferring what a program 'wants' — making agency hard to fully exclude.
